title: named control keys reach the pty raw
asserts: a `key` frame resolves NAMES to bytes in the core and writes them to the pty without bracketed paste, which is what makes them keystrokes rather than text: a Backspace erases the character before it and an Enter submits the line, so the title the stand-in then sets is proof both bytes were read by the line discipline and neither was pasted. An unknown name is refused with an `error` and writes NOTHING - the failure the frame exists to prevent is the word "Escape" landing in an agent's prompt box - and a key is never worth reviving a dead session for. And a C-c is a SIGNAL, not a byte that gets echoed: the child takes SIGINT and the core reports the exit, which is the half a core can pass the rest of this scenario while silently failing (juancode-toew).

steps.note: no trailing newline, and one character too many
a sequenced key acks like a sequenced input
the X is gone and the line ran, so 0x7f was ERASE and 0x0d was a carriage return - not the words Backspace and Enter typed into the line
one bad name in a batch, which refuses the whole batch
unlike an `input`, which revives a dead session to deliver a message: there is no prompt in a fresh process for a keystroke to answer
last, because it is meant to end the session

0x03 was INTR for the child's foreground group, not a character it read. exitCode -1 is the wire's "a signal took it" - an exit code of its own would mean the shell read the byte and fell out of its loop. The assertion this scenario was shipped without: both cores echoed the ^C, and only one of them delivered the signal, because a SIG_IGN the server installed for its own shutdown was inherited through exec into every pty child (juancode-toew).
